name: top4_loop08
text: # Biomedical Annotation Guidelines

name: top4_loop08
text: ## What to Annotate

name: top4_loop08
text: ### 1. Annotate all **Specific Disease** mentions

name: top4_loop08
text: A textual string referring to a disease name may refer to a **Specific Disease** or a **Disease Class**.

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Disease Class**: Mentions that could be described as a family of multiple specific diseases.

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Specific Disease**: Mentions that can be linked to one specific definition that does not include further categorization.

name: top4_loop08
text: **Referential anchoring test.**

name: top4_loop08
text: The label is decided by whether the phrase refers to a concrete, identifiable disorder, not by its surface form.

name: top4_loop08
text: - Annotate as **Specific Disease** when the phrase refers to a concrete disorder that is being diagnosed, manifested, or ruled out in a specific individual. This is signalled by a governing verb or prepositional frame such as "presenting with/as X," "distinguished from X," "has X," "affected by X," or "variant/form of X." It also applies when the phrase refers to a disorder defined by a specific gene, enzyme, or locus.

name: top4_loop08
text: - The label applies regardless of surface form. A condition-suffixed head noun, a plural count inflection, or a type-modifier-plus-head structure does not by itself make a phrase a Disease Class, and the label applies even when the phrase has no eponym, acronym, or proper name. The full mention span is treated as one unit, so a type modifier does not turn it into a subtype class (see "classical galactosemia," Example 15).

name: top4_loop08
text: - Plural number, suffix morphology, or coordination in a list is never sufficient on its own to assign either label.

name: top4_loop08
text: **Disease Class remains correct** when the phrase is used at the kind level, that is, as an indefinite generic predication (e.g., "is an autosomal recessive disease," "is a syndromal X-linked mental retardation") that does not refer to any particular patient or gene-defined disorder.

name: top4_loop08
text: Members of an unanchored feature list describing a syndrome category are handled under item 8.

name: top4_loop08
text: The predicate frame alone does not decide the label.

name: top4_loop08
text: In "Coats disease is characterized by ...", the subject names a particular disorder and is **Specific Disease**; the generic features in the complement are governed by item 8.

name: top4_loop08
text: **Precedence.**

name: top4_loop08
text: This rule does not apply to a disease-denoting expression that is an attributive premodifier of a non-disease head noun (e.g., "ovarian cancer cases," "the DTD gene").

name: top4_loop08
text: Those spans are **Modifier** mentions under item 3, which takes precedence over the referential test and its gene-defined clause.

name: top4_loop08
text: This rule does not alter the boundaries of Modifier or Composite Mention spans.

name: top4_loop08
text: **Example**

name: top4_loop08
text: > Diastrophic dysplasia is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by short stature, very short limbs and joint problems that restrict mobility.

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Annotate**:

name: top4_loop08
text: - “Diastrophic dysplasia” as **Specific Disease**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “autosomal recessive disease” as **Disease Class**

name: top4_loop08
text: ### 2. Annotate **contiguous text strings**

name: top4_loop08
text: A textual string may refer to two or more separate disease mentions.

name: top4_loop08
text: Such mentions are annotated with the **Composite Mention** category.

name: top4_loop08
text: A coordinated list of disease terms that functions as one mention is a Composite Mention.

name: top4_loop08
text: Coordination alone never turns a list of symptoms into a Disease Class (see item 8).

name: top4_loop08
text: **Example**

name: top4_loop08
text: > The text phrase “Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy” refers to two separate diseases.

name: top4_loop08
text: If this phrase is separated into two strings: “Duchenne” and “Becker muscular dystrophy,” it results in information loss, because the word “Duchenne” on its own is not a disease mention.

name: top4_loop08
text: ### 3. Annotate disease mentions that are used as **Modifiers** for other concepts

name: top4_loop08
text: A textual string may refer to a disease name, but it may modify a noun phrase (or may not be a noun phrase itself).

name: top4_loop08
text: In such cases, annotate using the **Modifier** category.

name: top4_loop08
text: **Example**

name: top4_loop08
text: > Although this mutation was initially detected in four of 33 colorectal cancer families analysed from eastern England, more extensive analysis has reduced the frequency to four of 52 English HNPCC kindreds analysed.

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Annotate**:

name: top4_loop08
text: - “colorectal cancer” as **Modifier**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “HNPCC” as **Modifier**

name: top4_loop08
text: **Narrower condition (takes precedence over items 1 and 7).**

name: top4_loop08
text: A disease-denoting expression is a **Modifier** when it specifies a non-disease head noun rather than naming the disorder itself.

name: top4_loop08
text: This includes:

name: top4_loop08
text: - an attributive premodifier of a case, patient, population, sample, study, family/kindred, series, risk, phenotype, gene, or allele noun (e.g., "ovarian cancer cases," "population-based ovarian cancer study," "ovarian cancer risk," "HNPCC kindreds," "ancient SLS genes," "the DTD gene," "G6PD deficient phenotype");

name: top4_loop08
text: - the complement of a history frame (e.g., "a family history of ovarian cancer").

name: top4_loop08
text: The Modifier label applies only when the disease expression functions as a modifier.

name: top4_loop08
text: If the disease expression is itself the head of the phrase, or stands as a complete entity (e.g., "Coats telangiectasis"), item 1 or item 7 governs.

name: top4_loop08
text: **Disease expression inside a nomenclature span.**

name: top4_loop08
text: When a disease-denoting expression (a full-form name whose head is a disease-category noun, or a short form that the document has explicitly defined as a disease) is an attributive premodifier of a non-disease head, label the disease-denoting substring **Modifier**, even when that head sits inside an out-of-schema nomenclature or proper-name construction (e.g., in "the Norrie disease gene (NDP)," "Norrie disease" is a Modifier).

name: top4_loop08
text: Assess that substring independently of the enclosing span, so that the span's out-of-scope status does not suppress the label.

name: top4_loop08
text: Leave non-disease material, such as the head noun or identifier ("gene," "NDP"), unlabelled.

name: top4_loop08
text: - Do not apply this rule when (a) the disease expression is itself the head of the phrase or stands as a complete entity, in which case the disease-class or specific-disease labels govern; (b) the enclosing name contains no disease-denoting substring, so the span is simply out of scope and remains O; or (c) a short form has no disease definition in the document, so it is not anchored as a disease reference and cannot be promoted to Modifier by position alone.

name: top4_loop08
text: **Specification versus post-modification.**

name: top4_loop08
text: A disease name that follows a non-disease noun through a "with" or "has" frame is not an attributive premodifier and is annotated as **Specific Disease** under item 1 (e.g., "63 kindreds with SLS").

name: top4_loop08
text: A disease name that is the disorder of which a form or variant is described (e.g., "the classical form of Coats disease") names the disorder itself and is **Specific Disease**.

name: top4_loop08
text: ### 4. Annotate **duplicate mentions**

name: top4_loop08
text: For each sentence in the PubMed abstract and title, the locations of all disease mentions are marked, including duplicates within the same sentence.

name: top4_loop08
text: ### 5. Annotate **minimum necessary span of text**

name: top4_loop08
text: Use the smallest span necessary to include all tokens expressing the most specific form of the disease.

name: top4_loop08
text: **Example**

name: top4_loop08
text: > In the case of “insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus,” the disease mention including the whole phrase was preferred over its substrings such as “diabetes mellitus” or “diabetes.”

name: top4_loop08
text: For enzyme-deficiency states (item 7), the span runs from the state head through the end of its prepositional complement and includes any enzyme name that premodifies the head, because those tokens express the most specific form of the disorder.

name: top4_loop08
text: ### 6. Annotate all **synonymous mentions**

name: top4_loop08
text: Abbreviation definitions such as “Huntington disease” (“HD”) are separated into two annotated mentions (one for the long form, one for the abbreviation).

name: top4_loop08
text: ### 7. Annotate **enzyme-deficiency states** that define a documented disorder

name: top4_loop08
text: IF a deficiency-type state noun (deficiency, insufficiency, deficit, or a noun that itself denotes reduced activity) is the head of a noun phrase, AND a following prepositional complement introduced by "of" or "in" names a biochemical or gene-product entity (enzyme, protein, or gene symbol) that is the defining molecular phenotype of a disorder described in the document, THEN label the entire span, from the state head through the end of the prepositional complement, as **Specific Disease**.

name: top4_loop08
text: The biochemical name inside the complement must not by itself cause an O label; the negative constraints below are the only exceptions.

name: top4_loop08
text: - "Defining" means an established characterization of the documented disorder. A deficiency offered as a hypothesized mechanism does not meet this condition.

name: top4_loop08
text: - The pathological qualifier must be carried by the head noun itself. A neutral head noun (activity, level, expression, function) qualified by a deficiency adjective (e.g., "deficient activity of X," "reduced level of X") is not a state head, and the span remains O.

name: top4_loop08
text: **Example**

name: top4_loop08
text: > “glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency”: the enzyme name premodifies the head, so the full string is one **Specific Disease** mention (Negative Constraint 2).

name: top4_loop08
text: **Negative constraints.**

name: top4_loop08
text: Do NOT apply this rule when:

name: top4_loop08
text: 1. The deficiency term is an adjectival modifier that does not head a disease noun phrase (e.g., “[enzyme]-deficient”). Label it **Modifier** (item 3).

name: top4_loop08
text: 2. The enzyme or gene name is a premodifier of the disease head (e.g., “[enzyme] deficiency”). The head is already the disease mention, and no prepositional restructuring applies.

name: top4_loop08
text: 3. The head is a bare symptom or sign noun, especially one in a coordinated list. This falls under the symptom-level convention (item 8).

name: top4_loop08
text: 4. The deficiency is reported as a generic biochemical observation and is not tied to a disorder described in the document. This includes in-vitro measurements on individual mutant constructs (e.g., “a severe reduction of FALDH enzyme catalytic activity when expressed in mammalian cells”) and hypothesized mechanisms (e.g., “we suggest that … results in a deficiency of X”). Keep the O label.

name: top4_loop08
text: 5. The state noun is premodified only by a generic word (e.g., “enzyme deficiency”) and its complement is an allele or variant designation (e.g., “in G6PD A-”). This is a variant-level biochemical description. The disorder is annotated through its named mention (e.g., “G6PD deficiency”), and the descriptive phrase remains O.

name: top4_loop08
text: ### 8. Annotate **generic manifestations and pathological states** as **Disease Class**

name: top4_loop08
text: IF a noun phrase’s head denotes a generic clinical manifestation (a sign, symptom, or discrete structural/developmental abnormality) or a generic pathological state (such as a deficiency or dysfunction of a biomolecule expressed through a prepositional complement), with no disease-type head noun and no proper-name disease label, AND the phrase is the complement of a predicate that characterizes a disease or causally links it to a disease-governed subject (e.g., “is characterized by,” “results in,” “is caused by”), THEN tag the full noun phrase, including its premodifiers and prepositional complement, as one **Disease Class** span rather than O.

name: top4_loop08
text: **Application conditions:**

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Predicate subject.** The predicate’s subject must be the disease, or a finding already attributed to the disease. A predicate whose subject is an etiological lesion that causes the disease (e.g., “a mutation in the NDP gene, which results in a deficiency of X”) does not license the label.

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Head-noun test.** Decide from the semantic role of the head noun (manifestation or state versus named entity), not from any particular symptom word or from the predicate verb alone. A neutral head carrying a pathological adjective does not qualify (see item 7).

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Processes excluded.** Developmental and pathophysiological process descriptions (e.g., “abnormal retinal vascular development,” or accumulation described as a mechanism step) are biological processes under What NOT to Annotate, item 5. Only discrete clinical findings are tagged.

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Symptom-level convention.** A bare, single-word sign or symptom noun that is a member of a coordinated list (e.g., “ichthyosis,” “spasticity”) remains O. Multi-word phenotype terms, including the grey-area terms “mental retardation” and “motor retardation” (Example 11), are Disease Class.

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Complement position only.** The noun phrase must be a complement of the characterizing predicate. A noun phrase that is the subject of a predicate (e.g., “WT1 dysfunction is implicated in …”) is not tagged.

name: top4_loop08
text: **Does NOT apply when:**

name: top4_loop08
text: - (a) the span is a named disease or uses a disease-type head noun (e.g., “[X] disease/syndrome/disorder/cancer,” or a named “[X] deficiency”), which is **Specific Disease** (item 1 or item 7);

name: top4_loop08
text: - (b) the span is only a gene, protein, or molecule name with no pathological qualifier, which is O;

name: top4_loop08
text: - (c) the predicate frame is present but the complement is not a manifestation or pathological state (e.g., a treatment, a population, or a neutral anatomical site), because the frame alone does not license the label;

name: top4_loop08
text: - (d) the span is a coordinated list of disease terms functioning as a single composite mention, which is **Composite Mention** (item 2);

name: top4_loop08
text: - (e) the head is a general term (e.g., “complications,” “abnormalities”), which is excluded under What NOT to Annotate, item 4.

name: top4_loop08
text: ## What NOT to Annotate

name: top4_loop08
text: 1. **Do not annotate organism names**

name: top4_loop08
text: - Organism names such as “human” were excluded from the preferred mention.

name: top4_loop08
text: - Viruses, bacteria, and other organism names were not annotated **unless** it was clear that the disease caused by these organisms is being discussed.

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Example**

name: top4_loop08
text: > Studies of biopsied tissue for the presence of Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus were negative.

name: top4_loop08
text: In this case: “Epstein-Barr virus” and “cytomegalovirus” are annotated as **Specific Disease** category **only** if the context clearly indicates the diseases they cause, otherwise not.

name: top4_loop08
text: 2. **Do not annotate gender**

name: top4_loop08
text: - Tokens such as “male” and “female” were only included if they specifically identified a new form of the disease.

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Example**

name: top4_loop08
text: > “male breast cancer”

name: top4_loop08
text: 3. **Do not annotate overlapping mentions**

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Example**: The phrase “von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease” is annotated as **one single disease mention** (Specific Disease category).

name: top4_loop08
text: 4. **Do not annotate general terms**

name: top4_loop08
text: - Very general terms such as “disease,” “syndrome,” “deficiency,” “complications,” “abnormalities,” etc. were excluded when used bare or without a specifying qualifier.

name: top4_loop08
text: - A qualified phrase that names a particular disorder is annotated (e.g., “C7 deficiency,” “Coats disease”) under items 1 and 7. Generic heads such as “complications” or “abnormalities” are not made into mentions by item 8.

name: top4_loop08
text: - However, the terms “cancer” and “tumor” were retained.

name: top4_loop08
text: 5. **Do not annotate references to **biological processes**

name: top4_loop08
text: - e.g. Terms corresponding to biological processes such as “tumorigenesis” or “cancerogenesis.”

name: top4_loop08
text: - This includes pathophysiological and developmental process descriptions (e.g., “abnormal retinal vascular development”), even when they are complements of predicates such as “is characterized by” or “results in” (see item 8).

name: top4_loop08
text: 6. **Do not annotate disease mentions interrupted by nested mentions**

name: top4_loop08
text: - Essentially, do not break the contiguous text rule.

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Example**

name: top4_loop08
text: > WT1 dysfunction is implicated in both neoplastic (Wilms tumor, mesothelioma, leukemia, and breast cancer) and nonneoplastic (glomerulosclerosis) disease.

name: top4_loop08
text: Here, the mentions “neoplastic disease” and “nonneoplastic disease” are not annotated because other tokens break up these phrases.

name: top4_loop08
text: 7. **Do not annotate non-disease deficiency descriptions**

name: top4_loop08
text: - Deficiency-type phrases whose head is a neutral noun (e.g., “deficient activity of fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase”), and generic or in-vitro biochemical observations, are not annotated even when an enzyme name is present (see item 7, Negative Constraints 1, 4, and 5).

name: top4_loop08
text: ## Precedence Between Overlapping Rules

name: top4_loop08
text: Where two rules above would label the same span differently, the narrower condition is applied first and the broader rule explicitly excludes it.

name: top4_loop08
text: 1. **Modifier before Specific Disease / Disease Class (item 3 before item 1).** A disease-denoting expression that is an attributive premodifier of a non-disease head, or that specifies a history frame, is a **Modifier** even when its referent is a concrete individual’s disorder. The referential test and its gene-defined clause in item 1 do not override this. A disease expression that is itself the head of a phrase is never a Modifier.

name: top4_loop08
text: 2. **Enzyme-deficiency before generic pathological state (item 7 before item 8).** When the item 7 conditions are satisfied, the span is **Specific Disease** and item 8 does not apply. Where item 7 is not satisfied (e.g., hypothesized mechanism, neutral head, generic or in-vitro observation), item 8 is evaluated on its own conditions. Its predicate-subject and head-noun tests keep such spans O unless every item 8 condition is met.

name: top4_loop08
text: 3. **Item 8 never overrides named disorders, composites, or general-term exclusions.** A named “[X] deficiency” or “[X] disease” remains **Specific Disease**. Coordinated lists of disease terms remain **Composite Mention**. Item 8 and the kind-level rule in item 1 both yield **Disease Class**, so they are consistent.

name: top4_loop08
text: 4. **Adjectival deficiency forms.** An adjectival deficiency form (“[enzyme]-deficient”) is a **Modifier** (item 7, Negative Constraint 1), not a Specific Disease.

name: top4_loop08
text: ## Examples

name: top4_loop08
text: 1. **“Insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Specific Disease**

name: top4_loop08
text: - Prefer the whole string.

name: top4_loop08
text: 2. **CDH1 mutations predispose to early onset “colorectal cancer.”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “early onset” may or may not be part of the disease mention, depending on:

name: top4_loop08
text: 1. If there is a UMLS concept specifying this as a separate form of disease

name: top4_loop08
text: 2. If the annotator believes it should be included

name: top4_loop08
text: 3. **Human “X-linked recessive disorder”**

name: top4_loop08
text: 4. **Her fresh serum lacked complement-mediated bactericidal activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae.**

name: top4_loop08
text: 5. **“Huntington disease” (“HD”)**

name: top4_loop08
text: - The long form and the short form constitute two separate mentions.

name: top4_loop08
text: 6. **C7 deficiency**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “This report represents the first cases of C7 deficiency associated with infectious complications.”

name: top4_loop08
text: - “infectious complications” is too general a term; C7 deficiency is a **Specific Disease**.

name: top4_loop08
text: 7. **“colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancers”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - Considered one **Composite Mention** of several Specific Diseases.

name: top4_loop08
text: 8. **WT1 dysfunction is implicated in both neoplastic (“Wilms tumor,” “mesothelioma,” “leukemias,” and “breast cancer”) and nonneoplastic (“glomerulosclerosis”) disease.**

name: top4_loop08
text: - Potential disease mentions include: “neoplastic disease,” “nonneoplastic disease,” “Wilms tumor,” “mesothelioma,” “leukemias,” “breast cancer,” and “glomerulosclerosis.”

name: top4_loop08
text: - “neoplastic disease” and “nonneoplastic disease” are **not** annotated because these phrases are interrupted by nested mentions.

name: top4_loop08
text: - “WT1 dysfunction” is the subject of the predicate, not a complement, so it is not a Disease Class mention (item 8).

name: top4_loop08
text: 9. **Tumorigenesis and cancerogenesis**

name: top4_loop08
text: - These refer to processes, not diseases.

name: top4_loop08
text: 10. **“autosomal recessive disease”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - Refers to a family of diseases that can be passed down genetically → **Disease Class** category.

name: top4_loop08
text: 11. **Large phenotypic variability with “convulsive disorders,” “motor retardation,” and “mental retardation.”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - These are “grey area” terms: they may not correspond to a single **Specific Disease**, so they are annotated as **Disease Class** category if appropriate (see item 8).

name: top4_loop08
text: 12. **Borjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome (BFLS) is a syndromal X-linked mental retardation.**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “Borjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome” = **Specific Disease**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “X-linked mental retardation syndrome” = a family of diseases (i.e., **Disease Class**)

name: top4_loop08
text: 13. **Acute meningococcal pericarditis**

name: top4_loop08
text: - Exists as a separate concept in UMLS.

name: top4_loop08
text: 14. **Acute Neisseria infection**

name: top4_loop08
text: - May or may not include “acute” depending on context.

name: top4_loop08
text: 15. **Classical galactosemia**

name: top4_loop08
text: - Includes “classical” because it corresponds to a particular form of the disease.

name: top4_loop08
text: 16. **Inherited spinocerebellar ataxia**

name: top4_loop08
text: - May or may not include “inherited,” depending on the annotator.

name: top4_loop08
text: 17. **“Adenomatous polyps of the colon and rectum”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Composite Mention**

name: top4_loop08
text: 18. **Fibroepithelial or epithelial hyperplasias**

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Composite Mention**

name: top4_loop08
text: 19. **Stage II or stage III colorectal cancer**

name: top4_loop08
text: - **Composite Mention**

name: top4_loop08
text: 20. **“the classical form of Coats disease”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “Coats disease” = **Specific Disease**. The phrase names the disorder whose form is described; “classical form” is not part of the mention.

name: top4_loop08
text: 21. **“a family history of ovarian cancer”; “ovarian cancer cases”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “ovarian cancer” = **Modifier** in both. In the first it is the complement of a history frame; in the second it is an attributive premodifier of a non-disease head.

name: top4_loop08
text: 22. **“63 kindreds with SLS”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “SLS” = **Specific Disease**. The “with” frame is post-modification, not an attributive premodifier.

name: top4_loop08
text: 23. **“the Norrie disease gene (NDP)”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “Norrie disease” = **Modifier**. “gene” and “NDP” remain unlabelled.

name: top4_loop08
text: 24. **“… is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by ichthyosis, mental retardation, spasticity, and deficient activity of fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “mental retardation” = **Disease Class** (item 8; multi-word grey-area phenotype term).

name: top4_loop08
text: - “ichthyosis” and “spasticity” = O (bare symptom nouns in a coordinated list).

name: top4_loop08
text: - “deficient activity of fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase” = O (neutral head carrying a deficiency adjective; item 7).

name: top4_loop08
text: 25. **“Coats disease is characterized by abnormal retinal vascular development, which results in massive intraretinal and subretinal lipid accumulation”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - “Coats disease” = **Specific Disease**.

name: top4_loop08
text: - The developmental and accumulation descriptions are pathophysiological processes and remain O (What NOT to Annotate, item 5).

name: top4_loop08
text: 26. **“a mutation in the NDP gene which results in a deficiency of norrin”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - O. The subject of “results in” is an etiological lesion, not the disease, and the deficiency is offered as a hypothesized mechanism (items 7 and 8).

name: top4_loop08
text: 27. **“diastrophic dysplasia (DTD) … the DTD gene”**

name: top4_loop08
text: - The defined short form “DTD” in parentheses is **Specific Disease** (item 6).

name: top4_loop08
text: - “DTD” as a premodifier of “gene” is **Modifier** (item 3, short form defined in the document).
